summary: This informational memo describes practices for accessing the same IMAP4 mailbox from multiple clients, reflecting existing servers and mailing list consensus. It does not define IMAP4 compliance.

plainLanguage.summary: When two people read the same mailbox, one of them can delete a message while the other is in the middle of asking for it. The protocol leaves it to the server to decide what happens. This memo sets out the choices a server can make, so that clients can be written to cope with any of them.

questions: what happens when an imap mailbox is deleted while in use
what is an imap expunge response
why should imap clients send noop
subtitle: What an IMAP4 server may do when several clients are using the same mailbox at once.

tldr.problem: When two people use the same mailbox, one of them deleting the mailbox or a message leaves the other with commands that no longer make sense.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the options an IMAP4 server has for deleting or renaming a mailbox and for expunging messages, and the matching rules a client should follow, such as issuing a NOOP after any failure to collect the pending expunge notices.
tldr.outcome: The protocol allows several server behaviours, so a client must be written against what the protocol permits rather than against one particular server, and this memo records what is common practice.

facts.label: Response code hinting at a new name

today: RFC 2180 is an Informational memo from July 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records common IMAP4 server practice for simultaneous access to a mailbox, and says that RFC 2060 must always be consulted to determine compliance, because the memo is not a definition of IMAP4 compliance and not an exhaustive list of valid behaviour.

sections.title: Why This Memo Exists and Its Conventions
sections.content:
IMAP4 is a rich client and server protocol that allows a client to access and manipulate electronic mail messages on a server. Within the protocol framework it is possible to have differing results for particular client and server interactions, and a protocol that does not allow for this is often unduly restrictive. For example, when multiple clients are accessing a mailbox and one attempts to delete the mailbox, an IMAP4 server may choose to implement a solution based on its own architectural constraints or on individual preference.

With that flexibility comes greater client responsibility. It is not sufficient for a client to be written on the basis of the behaviour of a particular IMAP server; rather the client must be based on the behaviour allowed by the protocol. The memo documents common IMAP4 server practice for the case of simultaneous client access to a mailbox, in the hope of ensuring the widest amount of interoperation between IMAP4 clients and servers. The behaviour described reflects the practice of some existing servers, or behaviour that the consensus of the IMAP mailing list has deemed reasonable, and is believed to be compliant with RFC 2060. It is not meant to define IMAP4 compliance, nor is it an exhaustive list of valid behaviour, and RFC 2060 must always be consulted to determine compliance, especially for server behaviour not described in the memo.

The conventions used in the examples are simple. C1, C2 and C3 indicate lines sent by three different clients connected to a server, and S1, S2 and S3 indicate lines sent by the server to client 1, client 2 and client 3 respectively. A shared mailbox is a mailbox that can be used by multiple users, and a multi-accessed mailbox is a mailbox that has multiple clients simultaneously accessing it. A client is said to have accessed a mailbox after a successful SELECT or EXAMINE command.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol deliberately leaves some choices open, which gives servers room to behave in the way that suits their own storage. The cost is that clients have to handle more than one possible answer.

sections.title: Deleting or Renaming a Multi-Accessed Mailbox
sections.content:
If an external agent or multiple clients are accessing a mailbox, care must be taken when handling the deletion or renaming of that mailbox. The memo lists four strategies a server may choose, and they are strategies rather than rules, so that a server can pick the one that suits it.

The first is to fail the DELETE or RENAME command of a multi-accessed mailbox. The server simply answers NO, for example "Mailbox FOO is in use by another user." This may not be practical, because if a large number of clients are accessing a shared mailbox the window in which no client has the mailbox accessed may be small or non-existent, which effectively renders the mailbox undeletable or unrenamable.

The second is to allow the DELETE command but keep the information in the mailbox available to the clients that currently have access to it. The mailbox is permanently removed when all clients have finished accessing it. For clients that do not already have access, the ghosted mailbox is not available: it would not be returned in a later LIST or LSUB command, and it would not be a valid mailbox argument to any other IMAP command, until the reference count of clients accessing it reached 0. In some cases this is not desirable, for instance when someone created a mailbox with offensive or sensitive information and would prefer the mailbox to be deleted and all access removed immediately rather than continuing until the client closes the mailbox. This behaviour may also prevent recycling of the same mailbox name until all clients have finished accessing the original mailbox.

The third is to allow the DELETE or RENAME and disconnect all other clients that have the mailbox accessed, by sending them an untagged BYE response. A server may often choose to disconnect clients in the DELETE case, but may implement a friendlier method for the RENAME case. The fourth is to allow the RENAME by simply changing the name attribute on the mailbox. Other clients that have access can continue issuing commands such as FETCH that do not reference the mailbox name, and they discover the renaming the next time they refer to the old mailbox name. Some servers may include the [NEWNAME] response code in their tagged NO response to a command that contained the old mailbox name, as a hint that the operation can succeed if it is issued with the new name.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things a server can do when asked to delete or rename a mailbox that someone else is using: say no, delete it later, kick the other users out, or just rename it and let the others find out.

sections.title: Fetching Messages That Have Been Expunged
sections.content:
If an external agent or multiple clients are accessing a mailbox, care must be taken when handling the EXPUNGE of messages. Other clients may be in the middle of issuing a command that depends on message sequence numbers. Because an EXPUNGE response cannot be sent while the server is responding to a FETCH, STORE or SEARCH command, it is not possible to notify the client of the EXPUNGE immediately, and this can leave ambiguity if the client then issues a FETCH, STORE or SEARCH on a message that has been expunged.

The memo's worked example has two clients with mailbox FOO selected, seven messages in the mailbox, messages 4 to 7 marked for deletion, and client 1 issuing an EXPUNGE for those messages. For a FETCH on those expunged messages, the server may keep them available to satisfy subsequent FETCH commands until it is able to send an EXPUNGE response to each client. The other client can then still fetch them, and learns of the expunges the next time it issues a command that allows the server to send them, for example a NOOP, after which the messages are no longer available. Keeping ghosted messages may not be desirable when a message contains offensive or sensitive information and immediate removal of access is preferred.

The second strategy is to return FETCH responses only for the non-expunged messages, together with a tagged NO. After a tagged NO FETCH response the client should issue a NOOP so that it is informed of any pending EXPUNGE responses, and can then either reissue the failed FETCH or, by examining the EXPUNGE response from the NOOP and the FETCH response, work out that the FETCH failed because of pending expunges. The third strategy is to return the usual FETCH responses for non-expunged messages, NIL FETCH responses for expunged messages, and a tagged OK. NIL FETCH responses are a representation of empty data as appropriate for the FETCH argument specified. If all the messages in the command have been expunged, the server should return only a tagged NO.

The memo notes one ambiguity with the third strategy: a client may not be able to distinguish between a NIL FETCH response caused by an expunged message and one caused by the data actually being NIL, for instance a FLAGS () response for a message with no flags set or for an expunged message. Where there is a potential ambiguity the client should issue a command such as NOOP to force the EXPUNGE responses to be sent. The fourth way to avoid the situation is for the server to fail the EXPUNGE of a multi-accessed mailbox altogether, which may not be practical if a large number of clients are accessing a shared mailbox, since the window in which there are no pending expunges may be small or non-existent.
sections.plainLanguage: A message that has been deleted is still referred to by number until the client is told. The server can keep it readable for a while, refuse the fetch, or return an empty answer, and the client has to be ready for all three.

sections.title: Storing, Searching and Copying Expunged Messages
sections.content:
For a STORE command on expunged messages the memo gives four more strategies. If the .SILENT suffix is used and the STORE completed successfully for all the non-expunged messages, the server should return a tagged OK, since the client has asked not to be told about each message. If the .SILENT suffix is not used and only expunged messages are referenced, the server should return only a tagged NO.

If the .SILENT suffix is not used and a mixture of expunged and non-expunged messages are referenced, the server may set the flags and return a FETCH response for the non-expunged messages along with a tagged NO, or it may return an untagged NO and set no flags at all. In both cases, after a tagged NO STORE response the client should issue a NOOP so that it is informed of pending EXPUNGE responses. In the first case the client may then reissue the failed STORE, or work out from the EXPUNGE responses and the FETCH responses that the STORE failed because of pending expunges. In the second case the client reissues the STORE command after updating its message list from any EXPUNGE response. If a large number of clients are accessing a shared mailbox, the window in which there are no pending expunges may be small or non-existent, which effectively disallows a client from setting the flags on all messages at once.

For SEARCH, a server may simply not return a search response for messages that have been expunged and that it has not yet been able to tell the client about. If a client expected a particular message to be in a search result and it was not, the client should issue a NOOP to see whether the message was expunged by another client.

COPY is the only IMAP4 sequence number command that is safe to allow an EXPUNGE response on, because a client is not permitted to cascade several COPY commands together: it must wait and confirm that the copy worked before issuing another one. A server may disallow the COPY of messages in a multi-access mailbox that contains expunged messages, and must then return the pending EXPUNGE responses and copy none of the messages, because if a COPY command is unsuccessful the server must restore the destination mailbox to its state before the attempt. Or the server may allow the COPY, return the pending EXPUNGE responses, and copy the messages that correspond to sequence numbers before any EXPUNGE response. The memo notes that the EXPUNGE response cannot take place until after the messages from the COPY command are identified, because of the rule that no expunge may be sent while commands are in progress.
sections.plainLanguage: The same problem comes up for commands that change flags, that search, and that copy mail. The client's rule of thumb is the same: if a command fails, ask for a NOOP so the server can tell you what has been removed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section says the document describes the behaviour of servers that use the IMAP4 protocol and so has the same security considerations as RFC 2060. In particular, some of the server behaviour described does not allow for the immediate deletion of information when a mailbox is accessed by multiple clients, and that may be a consideration when dealing with sensitive information where immediate deletion would be preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Where a server keeps deleted messages readable for a while, a message that should have been gone can still be fetched. That matters for sensitive mail.

cells: Allow DELETE and keep the data
Keeps the mailbox for the clients using it

items.title: NOOP after a failure
items.text: After a tagged NO, issue a NOOP so the server can send any pending expunge responses.

items.title: NIL FETCH responses
items.text: Empty data stands in for a message that has been expunged.

items.title: The reference count
items.text: A ghosted mailbox lasts until the last client closes it.

items.title: COPY is special
items.text: It is the only sequence number command that an expunge response may be sent with.

items.title: Do not cascade COPY
items.text: A client must wait for one COPY to finish before starting the next.

items.title: Restore on failure
items.text: If a COPY fails, the destination mailbox must be put back as it was.
